transcript:
Header: 2026-09-07 15:00 PDT | Duration 46m
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Tomás Ruiz (Redwood SE), Mark Hollis (Suncrest CTO), Sara Iqbal (Suncrest Head of ML), Javier Ortega (Infra), Leah Kim (Product)

[00:00] Alex Chen: hey everyone, thanks for making time. quick agenda — surface Suncrest goals, current infra, constraints, then run through quickstart vs dedicated/private and propose a pilot path, ok?
[00:20] Mark Hollis: yep thanks alex. we got 45 minutes, sara and javier will cover the ML and infra needs. we want to understand time-to-first-token because marketing wants a demo in 3 weeks.
[00:32] Sara Iqbal: hi all. goal is to add real-time product personalization at checkout. target latency under 150ms p95 ideally, and we need deterministic behavior during promos. also data residency for pII-related logs is a concern.
[00:46] Priya Nair: got it. couple clarifying q's — is the 150ms p95 measured end-to-end from your frontend or from your service to model? and what's the expected request size/sequence length?
[01:05] Javier Ortega: currently that's end-to-end, often the app-to-model is our bigger chunk. token lengths vary — usually small prompts, under 128 tokens. peak concurrency for personalization is about 600 qps during peak promo windows, sustained 150 qps.
[01:25] Alex Chen: perfect, that helps. two immediate paths: 1) PLG self-serve hosted API — fastest to get first token, we can give free credits and a sandbox, you can be live in hours for a demo. 2) Dedicated or Private — better for predictable throughput, VPC and KMS integration, but needs planning and provision time.
[01:45] Mark Hollis: budgetwise, we prefer starting with hosted to move fast, but concerns are compliance and seeing if p95 latency is achievable. plus the marketing demo will be in 3 weeks so we need the first token fast.
[02:05] Leah Kim: and also, if the hosted path looks good, we may still want to transition to Dedicated for the production rollout. want to understand the migration effort.
[02:20] Priya Nair: migration is supported — same API and client libs. typical path customers take: start hosted for proof-of-concept with free credits, then move to Dedicated when they need reserved capacity and VPC peering. Private on-prem is available for regulated workloads but takes more lead time.
[02:40] Sara Iqbal: any gotchas on model parity — will hosted vs dedicated give different response quality because of quantization or model variants?
[02:55] Tomás Ruiz: good q. models are functionally the same; dedicated may run a different optimized build or quant profile to save cost but we surface consistent endpoints. if you pin a model version that's maintained across modes. occasional kernel differences may slightly change perf but not semantics.
[03:22] Javier Ortega: about KMS — we run our own key management, need to ensure Redwood can integrate with our KMS or allow us to hold keys for private deploy.
[03:38] Alex Chen: yes we support customer-managed keys for Private and can integrate KMS for Dedicated in VPC setups. for hosted, we do offer bring-your-own-key with some constraints; i'll send the integration notes.
[03:55] Mark Hollis: what about audit logs and retention? important for PCI-sorta compliance of checkout touchpoints.
[04:10] Priya Nair: audit logs are available across all deployment modes. retention windows and log forwarding to your SIEM can be configured — for Private/Dedicated we can push logs into your S3 or Splunk instance.
[04:30] Sara Iqbal: ok. on latency — can you share any p95 numbers for 128-token requests on GPU instances for hosted? we have low tolerance for jitter during peaks.
[04:45] Tomás Ruiz: public benchmarks vary but for small prompts hosted can be ~60-120ms p95 depending on model and region. with Dedicated you can get more stable tails via pinned capacity and optimized kernels. We'll propose a benchmarking script for your 128-token profile.
[05:10] Mark Hollis: you mentioned free credits — what's in the sandbox package, and how long does it last?
[05:25] Alex Chen: sandbox includes $2k credits, a temporary sandbox org, access to the API keys, and a quickstart runbook. credits typically valid for 30 days; we can extend during an active pilot.
[05:40] Leah Kim: does sandbox allow load emulation to test concurrency or is it single-user only?
[05:50] Priya Nair: you can run load tests against the sandbox but we recommend we run a joint benchmark so we can ensure fair usage and avoid rate-limit noise. for load, Dedicated pilot is the more realistic test.
[06:05] Javier Ortega: what's the typical lead time for Dedicated? we need SLA for production.
[06:12] Alex Chen: Dedicated lead time is usually 4–6 weeks from contract/sign to capacity, depending on GPU type and region. SLA options are available post-provisioning. Private on-prem is longer.
[06:30] Mark Hollis: so for our demo in 3 weeks, hosted sandbox is the only practical route. fine — but we need to measure p95 and if jitter too high we'll escalate to Dedicated pilot.
[06:45] Sara Iqbal: also want to understand caching — we have a lot of repeated prefixes for recommendations, is prefix/KV caching supported?
[06:55] Tomás Ruiz: yes, automatic prefix caching and KV cache are part of the runtime. Redwood Optimize will suggest caching/batching profiles for your workload to reduce cost and improve latency.
[07:10] Mark Hollis: about costs — how do we estimate token cost for personalization? we need a model for compute + token unit for finance.
[07:25] Alex Chen: we'll share a cost model spreadsheet. large drivers are tokens per request, request rate, and whether you need lower-latency dedicated instances. We'll include example calculations for your 128-token average.
[07:45] Leah Kim: security review — can we run through high-level requirements now so you see where we stand?
[07:55] Mark Hollis: sure — SOC2, SSO (SAML/Okta), KMS, audit logs, data residency (EU for some customers). Also need a pen test or third-party attestation sometimes.
[08:15] Priya Nair: we have SOC2 reports and pen test summaries; SAML/Okta is supported for SSO, RBAC at token level, and data residency routing can be done with region pinning. we'll share docs.
[08:30] Javier Ortega: will there be network peering for Dedicated? we prefer VPC peering or PrivateLink rather than sending traffic over the public internet.
[08:40] Tomás Ruiz: Dedicated supports VPC peering and PrivateLink with customer-managed NAT gateways for egress. Private on-prem can be air-gapped with an appliance.
[08:55] Mark Hollis: how does Redwood handle graceful degradation if capacity is hit? our checkout cannot fail loudly.
[09:05] Alex Chen: smart routing/fallback policies can route to smaller model variants or queue requests. you can set fallbacks at the SDK layer for soft-degradation — e.g., cached response or a cheaper model for non-critical fields.
[09:25] Sara Iqbal: excellent. let's talk about success criteria for the pilot — for us success = p95 <150ms end-to-end on sample traffic, stable under 600 qps burst, result relevance parity with our baseline model, and audit logs available for demo.
[09:45] Alex Chen: noted. proposed pilot: 2-week sandbox + joint benchmark (we'll run synthetic traffic), then if results good, a 6-week Dedicated pilot with reserved capacity and VPC peering. does that sequence work?
[10:05] Mark Hollis: yes sounds pragmatic. pricing for Dedicated pilot?
[10:10] Alex Chen: pricing we will propose in the email — pilot discounts are common. I'll include Dedicated pilot daily capacity estimates and expected monthly commit ranges for budgeting.
[10:25] Leah Kim: migration effort — can you outline steps from hosted -> dedicated (we may want automated fallback during cutover).
[10:35] Priya Nair: yes, typical steps: 1) validate on hosted sandbox, 2) create Dedicated org and map models, 3) run canary traffic, 4) cutover with DNS or routing rules, 5) rollback policy implemented. we can share a playbook.
[10:55] Javier Ortega: one more infra detail — do we need to change client SDKs to switch modes?
[11:05] Tomás Ruiz: no code changes for standard API calls; just different endpoint and credentials. SDKs include routing logic and environment configs.
[11:25] Mark Hollis: ok, can you give concrete next steps now so we leave with a plan?
[11:35] Alex Chen: yes — we will 1) provision sandbox and send quickstart creds and runbook (priya), 2) send security materials and KMS notes (alex), 3) you share QPS and infra diagram (javier), 4) schedule pilot kickoff for week of 9/13.
[11:55] Leah Kim: timeline works, jami — i mean javier will send numbers. sara will prep sample prompts and evaluation set.
[12:12] Sara Iqbal: i'll prepare a 200-request eval set and annotate relevance metrics, share by 9/10.
[12:25] Alex Chen: perfect. i'll also attach a simple benchmark harness that you can run in your environment and we can run in parallel to compare.
[12:42] Mark Hollis: competitors — we've looked at MajorCloudAI and a vendor called SelfHostOps. MajorCloudAI had better tooling but pricing opaque; SelfHostOps requires too much ops. how do you compare?
[13:00] Priya Nair: Redwood focuses on predictable inference economics and unified ops across environments; we try to make migration frictionless and be transparent with benchmarks and cost models.
[13:20] Javier Ortega: question on observability — will we get per-token cost and trace to our tracing system?
[13:28] Tomás Ruiz: yes, Redwood Console includes token-level cost breakdowns, per-route latency, and traces. we also have tracing hooks to forward spans to your datadog or jaeger.
[13:42] Mark Hollis: good. any limitations in the sandbox we should know?
[13:50] Alex Chen: sandbox has soft rate limits to protect shared infra; we'll lift those for joint benchmarks. model catalog in sandbox will include common open models; if you need a private model, we can load it into a private pilot.
[14:05] Leah Kim: ok let's capture a few specifics for the email: security docs, sandbox creds, quickstart runbook, benchmarking script, and rough Dedicated pilot pricing.
[14:20] Alex Chen: we'll include those. any other questions?
[14:25] Mark Hollis: none on my side. thank you, this was helpful.
[14:32] Alex Chen: thanks everyone — recap and next steps in email.
[14:40] (call ends)
